value.mpe_verdict: Keep 0.16. The costed labour response is OpenResearch's individual non-transfer income fall per dollar transferred (ubi_model.MPE, [S14]), not the participation effect, so a revision of participation from 4.2 to 3.9 points does not by itself change it. Re-check the income estimate in the revised NBER paper (w32719 rev. 2): nber.org could not be reached from this session, so the income figure was not verified; if it moved roughly in proportion (3.9/4.2), the MPE would be about 0.15 (low 0.05 and high 0.29 cases unchanged).

value.omitted_benefit: Valued: Part 1 as Stage 2's base, A$0.09bn to A$0.37bn once at 3.9 points against the package, smaller against P* (not separately valued; ASSUMPTION close to nil). Not valued: universality's reach and payment channel (a value judgement; see break-even weights).

summary.unit: mixed: % of persons; million; A$bn; financial year; probability

value.P* re-costed: P* as first printed was not at Part 1 alone's budget: on the fiscal model's own basis it cost A$6.2bn more in 2028-29, because its child payment was costed against the household model's higher current FTB and was not charged its prior-year timing cost. Re-costed at Part 1's cost, P* pays A$6,750 a child a year (Part 1's supplement is A$7,452) and keeps the floor and Rent Assistance +75%.
value.Poverty: At the same cost as Part 1, P* cuts poverty after housing costs to 10.5% on the relative line, against 11.3% for Part 1 and 9.0% for the targeted package: 0.20 million fewer people in poverty than Part 1, and 0.40 million more than the package. Child poverty is 6.6% (Part 1 7.2%), sole-parent households 14.8% (16.4%) and people aged 67 and over 11.6% (12.1%).
value.Robustness: Across 9 household-model configurations (three random seeds and three calibrations), P* has less poverty than Part 1 in every group shown and a higher first-year net benefit in every one (A$0.8bn to A$3.1bn a year on the complete accounting); the targeted package has less poverty than P* in every group in every configuration.
value.Cost and borrowing: P* costs A$62.0bn in 2028-29 (1.86% of GDP), rising to A$130.8bn in 2045-46. The five taxes fall A$20.7bn short in the first year; that is borrowing, repaid with interest by 30 June 2032. Surpluses then build to A$45bn and are drawn down from the late 2030s.
value.The levy: On central yields a levy is first needed in 2043-44 (in 2044-45 if Rent Assistance grows on the fiscal model's path rather than with the model's rents), totalling A$37bn to 2045-46 and peaking at 0.62% of market income; Part 1's is 2044-45 and A$26bn. The five taxes must yield 100.2% of their costings for no levy before 2044-45.
value.Stress test: Drawing tax yield, behavioural responses, cost overruns, the household calibration and the AI path together, the chance of a levy before 2044-45 is 74% for P* (73% for Part 1) and before 2034-35 59% (58%); with symmetric uncertainty alone it is 48% and 37%. The most likely first levy year is 2032-33, when an advance not repaid by then would be levied at once. P* carries the same funding risk as Part 1; the package carries more.
value.A phased start: Starting the floor and Rent Assistance in 2028-29 and the child payment a year later removes the first-year borrowing: 2028-29 costs A$24.8bn against A$41.3bn of taxes, and on central yields no levy is needed to 2045-46. The price is a year without the child payment: A$26.4bn of family payments above the FTB families keep (a budget saving of A$37.3bn).
value.After housing costs: The no-worse-off rule protects payments under today's rules, not income after housing costs. In the paper's rent and interest-rate scenario, 1.11 million households on current payments (2.30 million people) are worse off under Part 1, by about A$933 a year; under P* 0.70 million (1.65 million people, about A$770): mostly Disability Support Pension households (0.28 million) and Age Pension households that own or are buying their home (0.26 million), whom Rent Assistance does not reach.
value.Poverty after the housing scenario: After the scenario's rent and interest-rate effects (central case), poverty on the relative line is 11.1% with P*, 11.7% with Part 1 and 9.8% with the package.
value.Who is better off after the taxes: Before the funding taxes 62% of households gain from P*; after them 35% are better off (33% by A$5 a week or more), against 33% under Part 1 and 42% under the package.
value.Net benefit: On the paper's complete accounting every design's first-year net benefit is negative at its 1.5 to 2.0 weights; it breaks even at a weight of 2.3 to 4.9 on gains to households in poverty for P* (2.8 to 6.1 for Part 1, 2.0 to 3.8 for the package). With the Green Book's standard weights every design is positive: P* A$40bn to A$49bn, Part 1 A$37bn to A$46bn, the package A$51bn to A$60bn, so standard weights widen the package's lead.
value.The trial's work-effort cap: At OpenResearch's revised 3.9-point fall in participation, the Australian trial would trip the 3-point cap with probability 0.79 to 0.84 (0.86 to 0.91 at 4.2). The costed labour response, 16 cents a dollar, is an income response and stays.
